Messages.Author: Chris Barnhart [Mr. Pynk]
Messages.Body:
> > In the same vein, Raven and Camille are not the same vamp, and it's
> > perfectly kosher to have both of them controlled at the same time.
>
> Officially, yes.
>
> Unofficially, though, it is totally unfair. The advantage gained by using
> both Raven and Camille is small, but statistically significant. If anyone
> cares to see, I have about 4K of archived information from the last time
> this came up.

Yuck! Statistics. :shudder: Jyhad isn't numbers. If you want numbers,
go play Magic. The concepts behind the cards... the idea that each card
represents something -- that what those last two vampires just did can be
imagined as a story -- is what gives Jyhad it's spark of life.

Do you really want to know what's wrong with degenerate decks (tap-bleed,
vote-pushing, etc.)? It's not that they win or that they're "unfair".
(they're not unfair, because anyone could counter with the same deck)
It's because those decks have DEGENERATED.

They are "degenerate" because someone has reduced the deck (and thus the
game) to NUMBERS. People have figured out formulae for winning, by
ignoring the concepts behind the cards.

Your statistical proof of something wrong with controlling Raven and
Camille is just as bad for the game as a Weenie Vote Push deck.

Chris Barnhart

> go play Magic. The concepts behind the cards... the idea that each card
> represents something -- that what those last two vampires just did can be
> imagined as a story -- is what gives Jyhad it's spark of life.

Yes, but the fact that Jyhad is a _balanced_ game is what makes it
worthwhile to play. Star Wars the CCG can be imagined as a story, as can
the Star Trek game, but neither are particularly balanced. While I agree
that game analysis (doing statistics, etc.) _in_ and during the game isn't
to exciting, between games, its nice to know that everything is kosher
rather than provably statistically biased.

> Do you really want to know what's wrong with degenerate decks (tap-bleed,
> vote-pushing, etc.)? It's not that they win or that they're "unfair".
> (they're not unfair, because anyone could counter with the same deck)

Null arguement. Since this game allows a variety of strategies, if one
strategy must be played to compete, it is still unfair, whether or not
anyone could do it.

> It's because those decks have DEGENERATED.

> They are "degenerate" because someone has reduced the deck (and thus the
> game) to NUMBERS. People have figured out formulae for winning, by
> ignoring the concepts behind the cards.

So your solution is...? Sit back and not complain about problems, hoping
the the Design Team doesn't make another mistake? Hope that the people
you play in a random game with somewhere don't play certain decks? Good
luck, because that's what you are wagering on.

I would rather try to show how there is an inequity (in this case, a
nearly 1/2 drop in self-contesting, and an over 75% drop in two people
contesting each other) in allowing Camille and Raven to be different
vampires.

This newsgroup has already caused several changes to official rules on
cards and other things. I don't mind continually trying.

> Your statistical proof of something wrong with controlling Raven and
> Camille is just as bad for the game as a Weenie Vote Push deck.

Why? Because on an intellectual level we think about how someone might
exploit the game? It doesn't matter then, that I hope to have the whole
fixed?

Well, I guess, you can always sit idly by hoping that someone doesn't
break your precious game and you don't play with people who exploit its
drawbacks, but I'll be trying to change it so that those problems don't
come up anymore.



Messages.Author: Gomi no Sensei
Messages.Body:
In article <Pine.BSF.3.91.960922...@server.wulaw.wustl.edu>,
Chris Barnhart [Mr. Pynk] <tvba...@server.wulaw.wustl.edu> wrote:

[raven v. camille recap]

>Yuck! Statistics. :shudder: Jyhad isn't numbers. If you want numbers,
>go play Magic. The concepts behind the cards... the idea that each card
>represents something -- that what those last two vampires just did can be
>imagined as a story -- is what gives Jyhad it's spark of life.

There's a difference between the *game* and the game's *design*. Jyhad's
appeal is (for some) based on its world, the characterizations -- the
game per se. For others, it's the elegance of the game's design. For most,
it's both. A game's premise (gameworld) can be fundamentally neat, and
if the design is flawed, the game is worthless (any White Wolf RPG will
do as an example -- beautiful premises, horrifying klugy designs). Vice
versa -- an excellently designed game won't survive if it doesn't have
an exciting premise. When we talk about stats and numbers here in the
newsgroup, we're exploring the game design, the balance that keeps Jyhad
from becoming a schlocky collection of crocks like Magic.

Little things add up. *This* card that was just a little out of line, but
basically ok, in expansion X combines with *that* card that was just a
little too cheap for its effect in expansion Y to become a Combo of Death --
witness the havoc wreaked on Magic by the combination of the fairly
innocuous (taken separately) Instill Energy/Animate Artifact/Time Vault,
which got Time Vault (a more or less balanced card on its own) banned in a
matter of weeks.

>Do you really want to know what's wrong with degenerate decks (tap-bleed,
>vote-pushing, etc.)? It's not that they win or that they're "unfair".
>(they're not unfair, because anyone could counter with the same deck)

That *is* magic. Land-strip is unfair, so you counter with your own
land-strip deck. Yawn. By forcing you to either play their strategy or
a specific, narrowly tuned counter-strategy, they're unfair.

>It's because those decks have DEGENERATED.
>
>They are "degenerate" because someone has reduced the deck (and thus the
>game) to NUMBERS. People have figured out formulae for winning, by
>ignoring the concepts behind the cards.

They've exploited holes in the game's design; therefore, it behooves us
to watch for development of such holes and endeavor to fix 'em. By analyzing
the existing cardset for biases and exploitable artifacts, we keep things in
balance.

>Your statistical proof of something wrong with controlling Raven and
>Camille is just as bad for the game as a Weenie Vote Push deck.

I'm afraid I must disagree. Not contesting Raven/Camille gives the Gangrel
a small, but definite, advantage over other clans. Just because it's not
a gamebreaker is no reason to let it slide.

gomi

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
Jason Burke <jbu...@oneimage.com> writes:

>Chris Barnhart [Mr. Pynk] wrote:

>> They are "degenerate" because someone has reduced the deck (and thus
>> the game) to NUMBERS. People have figured out formulae for winning,
>> by ignoring the concepts behind the cards.

You have to remember that no matter what Jyhad is based on, it IS a game.
The cards are what the cards are; they are not proxies for a "real-life"
thing. It would be more accurate to say people are winning by not being
confused by what they think the cards should do.

>WooHoo! Way to go! Amen! I totaly agree, it's these types of people
>that make the game unfun, unfair, and totaly lifeless. Though in
>Adrian's defense I will say that I dont truely believe he is
>in this category. Maybe a tab bit over-concerned with game balance,
>not in the lifeless category though.

In a CCG, I don't think it's possible to be *too* concerned about game
balance. CCGs are incredibly intolerant of balance mistakes. In most
games, if there's a balance mistake, it's usually controlled by there
being only one of them in a game set but with CCGs even the rarest cards
are ususally printed by the thousands, and whoever starts buying them can
have a great advantage. You can errata and restrict them to your heart's
content, but the card will *always* have the original printing on it.
Worse, even if you put out a new edition the old cards are still there.
So even one moderate mistake on one card out of hundreds can wreck the
game forever.

Another point is the incredible size of the game spaces of these games.
The potential number of decks for any of these games will be at least a
googol (10^100). You can't test the whole thing, one mistake can ruin the
game -

You'd better be careful about balance issues.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)
